comments.text:
Andrew Michael 144hz is a way more noticeable improvement than 1440p is.

1440p is just a higher resolution, so it requires less antialiasing and generally looks better.

144hz is just a higher refresh rate (amount of times your screen updates the image per second) so motion looks significantly smoother than 60hz.

If you have 1070 you should consider getting a monitor that can do 1440p 144hz because that is a very strong video card.

Basically, it's a mainstream RX 480 that has the power of a R9 390.

comments.text:
Actually the Pascal cards are 16nm, though AMD will be able to save more money making their 14nm than Nvidia's 16nm.

CPU wise, Intel is said to have custom made designs every time they make a new product, so it's very expensive to churn out chip die very often.


The Price-Performance point is very important for AMD.

If they push for a RX 480 which is said to be equivalent to a R9 390, and Nvidia's GTX 970, at $200. This means a $250-300 GPU that would be called the RX 480X, 490/X, etc, would provide an EVEN greater price-performance competitive edge.

How much is that GTX 1070 going to cost?
$400? GTX 1080? $700-800?

AMD can push for equivalent performance at a much lower price if they slowly scale their new GPU up, easily stealing the market for low to mid level gpu markets.

comments.text:
I have done an SLI 970 averages in a couple of games @3440x1440 minus Overwatch @2560x1440. Here they are:

BF4:  min: 63 Max: 173 AVG: 109  (MAX SETTINGS)   

GTAV Benchmark: Min: 61 Max: 271 AVG: 130 (Very High)   
GTAV Gameplay: Min:  23 MAX: 270 AVG: 105 (Believe the low 23 is due to the RAM limitation at VERY HIGH graphics for GTAV as it game a lot of stutters)

Star Wars BF: min: 54 Max: 114 AVG: 91 (Max Settings)   

Overwatch: Min: 104 MAx: 222 AVG: 162 (max settings)    

All games were tested in IN-GAME environments with Multiplayer besides GTA V. I would not run all very high with GTA V, put some settings on high and you will be golden. But as you can see 970 SLI still proves to be the king until better driver support and 3rd party cards. 

In my opinion, if you have a 970 and can run SLI pick up another 970 because right now it is faster than the 1080. Down the road with better driver support... only time will tell.

comments.text:
There are some DX12 games where even the R9 390 competes with the 980 TI. Don't single out DX12 just yet, it's still in early stages and can give great fps gains if fully utilized. It doesn't always work yet though, but in the future it will give us better fps and graphics at the same time, which is all that we should really care about.

Overall 980 TI is still FAR more consistent (in some games even an OC'd 980 beats Fury X), has far better OC and is just all around safer for now, but not as future proof (compare 290x to 780 TI, 780 TI used to be better but not anymore). If I had the choice between Fury X and 980 TI, I'd still get a 980 TI since even in AMD favoured games you can OC it to Fury X levels, or at least very similar performance so the OC makes it superior to the 780 TI, which never really hit stock 980 performance and gets beaten by the 970 regularily, sometimes by embarassing amounts. I just hope for Maxwell users that the 980 TI stays consistent.

Now the RX 480 is an absolute beast for that price if the early benches are correct (Doom at 1440p, 3DMark showing its between the 980 and Fury). If you only care about performance 1070 is still a whole class above it and the way to go, but if you want price/performance get the RX 480 since it's not that too far from the 1070. It's like comparing a 980/Fury to 980 TI, yes the 980 TI is obviously better but the 980/Fury are no slouch either, even for 1440p.

comments.text: Hey! Well I think you need more power supply for something like that. Like 750W is probably a sweet spot. I went a little overkill with my rig and got 1000W just for further upgrades, but you dont need that much, even with SLI (2 graphics cards). Other then that I can suggest that you get a 2tb hdd (hard drive) if you want, since its not that big price difference for twice the storage (if you need it). Other then that advice it looks like a very nice PC that will last for years. Just make sure that the motherboard supports DDR4 memory and that the socket on the CPU is the same as the motherboard so everything fits. Monitor, hmm. Well you can buy a cheap full HD (1920x1080p) monitor and with this computer run everything on high/ultra quality. It's overkill for that resolution, but it will last you a long time. If you are coming from a console it's probably a big upgrade to get full HD at 60 fps. If you have more budget for a monitor you could buy a 1440p one, which is the sweet spot in my opinion. Higher resolution that looks great and should be playable at a high framerate as well. I don't know if you want 1 screen or more, I think its nice to have 2, but it depends if you multitask a lot. comments.text:
6:04 Have you guys been keeping up with Polaris news? IT IS NOT going to compete with the 1080 or 1070 - at least not Polaris 10 which is the biggest and most powerful Polaris currently annoumced, with 2560 SPs, it would APPEAR that it simply cannot compete against top tier cards.

In fact even AMD seems to suggest that Polaris is not meant to COMPETE with the GTX 1080/70, it is meant to fill in the gaps between cards like the 960 to 980 and Pascal cards. With AMD basically saying as much and also saying that Vega will be the GPU to compete and possibly surpass Pascal.


I mean, I hope AMD does get SOME kind of top tier offering that is not such a MASSIVE flop as the Fury cards, as that is what it WILL take for AMD to continue clawing back market share.


The R9 390/390X were doing EXACTLY that because when compared against the 970 and 980 - they were definitely the best price to performance option - at the time... I have ALREADY found 980s for as cheap as $280 and 980ti's as cheap as about $380 respectively, which is going to QUICKLY take the "Value" out of the 390/390X. 

And then there are the Furys, with the 1080 AND 1070 beating them STRONGLY at fully STOCK speeds (and Fury cards DO NOT OVER CLOCK WELL) - even in Ashes of the Singularity with Async and DX12 - by a rather large margin!

So, I hope AMD has more up their sleeves than they have let on. I would HONESTLY love to buy a Radeon card again for the first time since my X850. But it MUST BE able to compete for me to do so!


And then there is the whole Tesselation factor, I forget the EXACT numbers (I shall look them up again shortly) but IIRC, a GTX 770 can do far more Tesselation calculations per second than a FURY X!

And I know there are many examples of WASTEFUL amounts of tesselation in games, but that does not change the fact that AMD cards will choke unless the Devs or drivers have some kind of option to turn down the tesselation factor, and that is just another worry of mine when considering Radeon. There is also driver support, DX11 performance, a myriad things that I would not know first hand, being my last Radeon was the X850 well before hardware tesselation was even a thing...
comments.author: @Dysphoricsmile

comments.text:
The AMD RX 480 has over 5 TFlops of performance.
It's not directly competing at the level of GTX Titan, but at mid-high levels like the Fury X.

The fact is, Polaris is a 14nm gpu, it has a ton of additional areas to tweak and boost performance, where as the 1070s series are still using the older 28nm chips, meaning Nvidia relies mainly drivers and software to keep those performance high.

And lower cost GPU is a bigger factor than a high end GPU that less people would buy. It lets AMD make some cash to further fund their attempt at more powerful cards down the line.

What's interesting is that AMD has 14nm FinFET chip, not a regular 14nm or even 16nm chip that Nvidia will try to roll out. These are chips that will also be used in smartphones and the likes, like the next generation consoles.

You would be surprised how cost factors into the gaming industry, as the people who can afford to pay over $1000 to create or upgrade their rigs are a really tiny minority.

Intel started to promote their Broadwell-E chipset and cpus, if you can afford building a 1500-3000 dollar PC that is.

This was kinda confusing, but heres how I'm understanding it.
Nvidia set an MSRP for the 1080 in general. 

The 'Founders Edition' Is just Nvidia's 'own design'.
It's the same concept as MSI's "Twin Frozr", or Gigabyte's "Windforce".
However, unlike the Twin Frozr, or Windforce, any board manufacturer can use the cooler's design. I'm not sure if those other manufacturers are allowed to say "Founders Edition" or not.
Ive read things like they don't want to call it reference because that implies its baseline. Which it kinda is... Why would anyone make/sell a heatsink that was worse then it I have no idea. (Unless it was a ITX version or something.)

Now the reason it's priced  higher? Well as far as I am aware, Nvidia doesn't want to piss off the board manufacturers by low balling the price.
It's kinda like why the console digital versions of games aren't cheaper then their physical counterparts. Sony/Microsoft/Nintendo don't wanna piss off Gamestop, Best Buy, exc.

comments.text: It is always better to play at the native resolution of the monitor, unless you're doing something like super sampling, but even then you're still technically still at the native resolution.  If you're trying to put a 3880x1620 image on a 1440p monitor, you have to shrink it down to see the entire image. When you shrink it down the gpu (or cpu or the image processor in the monitor, I don't remember which but it's probably the gpu) has to decide what pixels to send to the monitor to make a 1440p image. It will sometimes look worse than running at 1440p. The exception is super sampling and if the custom resolution is a perfect ration to the monitors native resolution (4k to 1080 is an exact 4:1 ratio). Linus or Luke explained this somewhere a lot better than I just did.

comments.text:
Yes, 1070 degrees is just leass than 3 full rotations (3 x 360 degrees = 1080 degrees), but you are incorrect in your use of Radians.  Radians are an other unit for angular measurements.

Pi does not equal 1 Radian.  180 degrees equals Pi  Radians, thus 1 Radian = 180/Pi ~ 57.3 degrees.

Also, by definition, 1 Radian is the angle that subtends a circular arc equal in length to the radius of the circle.  The curvature of the subtended arc is why 1 Radian is just a bit less than 60 degrees which is the size of the angles in an equilateral triangle.  

(Think of compressing one of the corners (vertex) of an equilateral triangle to bring tow adjacent sides closer together.  This makes the opposite side bulge outward if it keeps the same length.  Compress the vertex until the angle is ~ 57.3 degrees or 1 Radian and the opposite side will be curved outward in the shape of a part of a circle's circumference.)
